newsitem.title: FRANCE: International donors generous on Sierra Leone aid.
newsitem.headline: International donors generous on Sierra Leone aid.

text.p: International donors have pledged a generous $640.6 million in aid to Sierra Leone, more than the impoverished west African nation had sought to help it recover from a five-year rebel uprising, the World Bank said on Friday.
Sierra Leone Finance Minister Thiamu Banguru had requested $589 million in aid from a World Bank consultative group to help it promote sustainable economic development and combat poverty.

"This is a resounding endorsement of the course Sierra Leone has embarked upon," Mamadou Dia, World Bank country director for Sierra Leone, told reporters after a two-day meeting of the consultative group which began on Thursday.
"I was pleased with the outcome of the meeting," added Banguru. "What impressed me most was the confidence which they (group members) had in the present administration".

Dia said donors were particularly impressed by Freetown's success in bringing down inflation to six percent last year from over 100 percent in 1990-91 and nearly halving the budget deficit to 6.3 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) last year from 12 percent in 1989.

The nation, one of the world's poorest, though rich in diamonds and other minerals, has also implemented far-reaching structural reforms and made great progress in reducing public payroll corruption since the rebel Revolutionary United Front agreed to lay down arms last year, Dia said.

Dia noted that the advent of peace had raised citizens' expectations and stressed the importance of moving quickly to heal the wounds left by the war and maintain economic stability to improve standards of living.

Banguru adviser Jim Funna said World Bank projections of 10.2 percent GDP growth in 1997, 14.8 percent growth in 1998 and 8.7 percent growth in 1999 were "realistic" but added that growth would taper off somewhat after 1999.

He said the strong growth would be driven by a resumption of mining activity and a "quick action programme" designed by the United Nations in September 1996, under which $273 million would be pumped into the economy over two years.

The money for the quick action plan is to come from the $640.6 million in aid which has just been pledged. The total aid package includes $274.7 million in grants, $23.8 million in debt relief and $342 million in loans on concessional terms.
Funna said Freetown intended to court foreign investment by drafting a new investment code, revamping national company laws.
"We should have a new investment code in place before the end of this year," he told reporters.
He said Sierra Leone's external debt totalled roughly $1.08 billion for 1995-96.

That included $595.8 million owed to multilaterals like the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank, $87.4 million in short-term debt and $328.6 million in bilateral debt, most of it owed to Britain, Austria, Switzerland and France, Funna said.
